title_eng: Postoperative Pain Assessment Model Based on Pulse Contour Characteristics Analysis
title_kor: Postoperative Pain Assessment Model Based on Pulse Contour Characteristics Analysis
abstract:
IEEE JOURNAL OF BIOMEDICAL AND HEALTH INFORMATICS, VOL. 23, NO. 6, NOVEMBER 2019 2317
Postoperative Pain Assessment Model Based on
Pulse Contour Characteristics Analysis
Hyeon Seok Seok, Byung-Moon Choi, Gyu-Jeong Noh, and Hangsik Shin , Member, IEEE
Abstract— This study aims to develop a new postop-
erative pain assessment model based on pulse contour
analysis and to evaluate its effectiveness in postoperative
pain assessment. We derived candidate features from pho-
toplethysmography (PPG) and developed an assessment
model based on multiple logistic regressions with a combi-
nation of features. This study also includes investigations
into the optimal unit of analysis and number of features.
For model development, PPGs obtained from 78 surgical
patients with a six-min duration in pre- and post-operation
conditions, including a training set of 56 pairs and a test set
of 22 pairs, were used. We tested models with 5, 10, 20, 30,
40, 50, 60, 70, and 80 beats as an analysis unit, and with 1 to
8 of features for optimization, then determined 20 beats and
three features to be the simplest optimal unit of analysis and
number of features, respectively. The selected features were
RMSSD-ACVonset /ACAbl , AV-Asys /Atotal , and SD-RS,w h e r e
RMSSD-ACVonset /ACAbl is the root mean square of the suc-
cessive difference of the ratio of pulse onset amplitude to
the pulse onset-to-peak amplitude, AV-Asys /Atotal is the av-
erage value of a normalized systolic area of a pulse with a
total pulse area, and SD-RS is the standard deviation of a
rising slope of a pulse. The accuracy (AC) and the area un-
der the curve (AUC) of the proposed model were 0.793 and
0.872 in the development set ( N = 56), respectively, which
were superior to those of SPI (AC: 0.643, AUC: 0.716) and
ANI (AC: 0.633 AUC: 0.671). In the test set ( N = 22), the AC
and AUC of the proposed model were 0.712 and 0.808, re-
spectively, which were superior to those of SPI (AC: 0.640,
AUC: 0.709) and ANI (AC: 0.640, AUC: 0.680).
Index Terms — Classiﬁcation, pain assessment, photo-
plethysmography, postoperative pain.

I. I NTRODUCTION
E
IGHTY percent of surgical patients experience postoper-
ative pain; moreover, 88% of these patients complain of
mode rate or more pain [1]. Severe postoperative pain, deﬁned
as /22658 visual analogue scale (V AS) score or numerical rating
scale (NRS) score, could induce extreme discomfort and sig-
niﬁcantly reduce a patient’s quality of life [2]. Postoperative
pain can be relieved using opioids. However, overdosing on
analgesics could cause life-threatening adverse effects, such as
prolonged sedation or prolonged respiratory insufﬁciency [3],
[4]. Clinical ﬁndings in patients with opioid analgesic overdose
include respiratory depression, miosis, stupor, hepatic injury
from acetaminophen or hypoxemia, myoglobinuric renal fail-
ure, rhabdomyolysis, absent or hypoactive bowel sounds, com-
partment syndrome, and hypothermia [5]. Moreover, chronic
pain syndromes may increase the levels of stress hormones and
sympathetic activity [6], [7]. Despite the importance of proper
dosing with analgesics, self-dosage amounts of opioids cannot
be formalized because the pain experience depends on each
patient’s condition as well as environmental and emotional con-
ditions. This is also because indices such as anxiety sensitivity
and distress tolerance closely related to pain experience show
inter-individual differences. In fact, pain experience itself even
has intra-individual differences.
Because pain is a subjective experience, self-reporting pain
assessment metrics such as V AS or NRS have been regarded
as the gold standards of pain assessment [8]. The V AS consists
of a straight line of 100 mm scale with the endpoints deﬁning
extreme limits of pain intensity: no pain, score of 0; and pain
as bad as it could be or worst imaginable pain, score of 100 [9].
NRS uses an 11-, 21-, or 101-point scale for patients’ subjective
pain intensity expressed through a speciﬁed number [10]. Both
pain-rating scales are appropriate for use in clinical practice,
but cannot be applied in patient groups comprising preverbal
children or cognitively impaired individuals [10], [11]. Thus, the
development of a more accurate and objective pain assessment
method is necessary for controlling appropriate opioid dosages
following surgery.
In an attempt to quantify pain, the surgical pleth index (SPI,
GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA), analgesia nociception index
(ANI, MDoloris Medical Systems, Loos, France), and pupillom-
etry have been developed. SPI is based on photoplethysmogram
amplitude (PPGA) and heart beat interval (HBI) as measured
by photoplethysmography (PPG), which are correlated with
the sympathetic response to surgical stimulation [12]. SPI is

calculated using the following equation: 100-(0.67× PPGAnorm
+ 0.33 × HBInorm ) where PPGAnorm and HBInorm are normal-
ized PPGA and normalized HBI, respectively. The SPI value
ranges between 0 and 100, indicating very low and very high
surgical stress responses, respectively. Several studies have re-
ported that SPI is a potential indicator of pain assessment in un-
conscious patients [12]–[14]. However, SPI has been reported to
show limited accuracy in assessing conscious subjects, because
the SPI algorithm is based on patients under anesthesia [15]. ANI
quantiﬁes surgical pain based on heart rate variability (HRV),
which is derived from standard electrocardiography (ECG) [16].
ANI is derived from the parasympathetic component of HRV
and respiratory sinus arrhythmia [17]. ANI ranges between 100
and 0, representing a low-stress level and high-stress level, re-
spectively. It has been reported that ANI responds to surgical
stimuli under anesthesia [18], [19]. However, following surgi-
cal stimulation, ANI showed large inter-individual variability
in values [20]. Reﬂex pupillary dilatation (RPD) is related to
subjective pain assessment in wakeful patients and shows corre-
lation with postoperative pain [21], [22]. RPD has been reported
to be a superior indicator of nociceptive stimulation over tradi-
tional pain indicators such as heart rate and blood pressure [23].
However, correlation analyses between pupillary responses and
self-reported postoperative pain scores have shown inconsistent
results [22], [24], [25].
Attempts have been made to apply machine learning to var-
ious biomedical applications, but none of these cases have in-
volved direct application to postoperative pain evaluation. Re-
cently, a study has been performed to predict persistent post-
surgery pain from preoperative cold pain sensitivity using a
machine learning technique [26]. However, this study only de-
pended on a simple binary classiﬁer, and did not show the appli-
cation of a recent machine learning technique. Rather, it suggests
that the selection and proper application of a suitable classiﬁer
is necessary in the future.
Photoplethysmography is a non-invasive method for mea-
suring blood volume changes at peripheral body sites such as
the ﬁngertips, earlobes, or wrists by irradiating light of a spe-
ciﬁc wavelength and detecting the amount of transmitted or
reﬂected light [27]. PPG waveform has a systolic peak and
pulse onset which indicate maximal blood volume by contrac-
tion of the heart and minimal blood volume by relaxation of
the heart, respectively. PPG waveform analysis is used to an-
alyze various physiological phenomena, such as variations of
peak intervals and blood volume, as well as estimations of
blood pressure and cardiac output [28], [29]. In pain assess-
ment, PPG is regarded as a potential indicator because it can
estimate changes in blood volume, which are inﬂuenced by the
response of the autonomic nervous system under pain stimuli
[30], [31].
The purpose of this study is to propose a new postop-
erative pain assessment metric based on PPG waveforms.
PPG waveform-based candidate features that may be re-
lated to postoperative pain are extracted and veriﬁed. Fi-
nally, a new postoperative pain assessment model is pro-
posed. The overall procedure of this research is presented in
Fig. 1.
Fig. 1. Overall procedure of this research: Preprocessing, feature ex-
traction, feature selection and classiﬁcation, and evaluation.
II. M A TERIALS AND METHODS
A. Dataset
The study was approved by the Asan Medical Center In-
stitutional Review Board (approval number: 2016-0477) and
registered on the international clinical trials registry platform
(http://cris.nih.go.kr, KCT0002080). All participants provided
written informed consent for their participation in the study. A
total of 81 subjects were enrolled, of which three were excluded
due to a failed recording. Ultimately, data from 78 subjects (31
males, 47 females, 51.8 ±10.9 years) were used for analysis.
Patient characteristics and the type of surgery are described in
Table I.
PPG, SPI, and ANI were simultaneously recorded in pre- and
post-operation. Pre-operative data were recorded in the surgery
waiting room immediately prior to surgery. First, the 100 mm
V AS was recorded, and the PPG and SPI were simultaneously
recorded for 6 min. Post-operative data were recorded after
the patient was transferred to the recovery room immediately
following the operation. We conﬁrmed that 0 V AS was observed
in the pre-operation condition, while >60 V AS was observed
in the post-operative condition. At the time, PPG and SPI were
recorded for 6 min after ﬁrst recording V AS. Opioids were
not used for 6 min immediately after surgery, and were then
administrated upon completion of signal measurement.
PPG was measured on the index ﬁnger of the opposite arm
with intravenous therapy at a sampling frequency of 300 Hz.
SPI was recorded every 10 seconds and ANI was recorded every
second. Among the 78 patients, SPI and ANI recording failed
in 13 and three subjects, respectively. Carescape © R
B850 (GE
Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) was used to record PPG and
SPI. ANI Monitor (MDoloris Medical Systems, Loos, France)
was used to record ANI.
